newsitem.title: SPAIN: FORECAST - Spain's CPI seen hitting a low in May.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - Spain's CPI seen hitting a low in May.

text.p: Spanish inflation moderated more than expected in January, continuing its steady downtrend, but economists said on Thursday it could change direction after touching a low in May or June.

Better-than-expected January CPI -- up 2.9 pct year-on-year after 3.2 percent in December with core inflation rising at a tame 2.8 percent -- showed that the government had already reached its first-quarter goal.
Many economists believe Spain could easily reach its target of ending 1996 at 2.6 pct, but they also said there is little room for the inflation to improve further from here.

"We see inflation dropping sharply and touching a low in May, around 2.0 percent, but thereafter it will pick up to around 2.7 pct in December, and will average three percent in 1998," said Antoni Espasa, economist at University Carlos III in Madrid.
The mild January data was mainly due to an already-expected fall in olive oil and energy prices, but the breakdown of the actual data revealed worrying signs.

"The fall in the year-on-year is mainly due (0.28 percent out of the total fall of 0.3 percent) to processed food, and a lot of this (around 1.5 percent) is due to olive oil," said an analyst in a large Spanish bank.
The decline in olive oil prices was already expected by analysts, although it was foreseen for later this year.

"I think (the decline in core CPI) is due mainly to the fall in processed food. That means olive oil declines had a greater-than-expected effect but I do not think this will change the whole picture for the year," said Espasa.
Core inflation excludes energy and fresh food prices, but includes processed food.
Another factor behind the fall in January CPI was energy prices, which rose 4.6 percent year-on-year versus 6.5 percent in December, given a decline in electrical tariffs.
"Energy prices showed a very good trend," said Maria Victoria Nunez, junior economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
But worrying signs were coming from general services, which were at 3.5 percent in January after 3.4 percent, and from prices of durable goods, which were at 2.4 percent from 1.3, analysts added.
"The CPI breakdown suggests the Bank of Spain would prefer to wait before easing its monetary policy," said Colin Warren, economist at Tokai Bank in London.
Earlier this week, the Bank of Spain's latest report said a slowdown in service prices may have bottomed out while energy prices may be picking up.
"The big jump in durable consumer goods is mainly due to personal transport, and I think this is due to higher car prices," said an analyst.

The upward pressure on service prices is likely to remain until structural reforms are put into place. Spanish trade unions and employers are in talks aimed at reforming a labour market, which is considered over-regulated.
"I think the Bank of Spain could decide to wait for the labour reform before moving its rate lower," said Tokai's Warren.
Therefore, Spanish inflation is expected to decline steadily in the first five months of this year, particularly because of a favourable comparison with last year's high rates.
But this won't be the case in the second part this year, or in 1998.
